chunks: "A differential pair is two traces that carry complementary versions of the same signal: when one goes up by a bit, the other goes down by the same amount, and the receiver only looks at the difference between them.
So the information is V P minus V N and the average of the two, the common-mode level, doesn't carry data. That's useful for three reasons.
Noise that couples into the pair, like crosstalk, ground bounce or EMI pickup, hits both lines about equally, so it's common-mode and the receiver subtracts it out.
Second, the currents in the two lines are equal and opposite so their fields cancel and the pair radiates less.
And third, you get twice the voltage difference for a given swing per line, so you can run lower swings, which also helps with speed and power.
The trade-offs are cost and discipline.

You need twice the pins and twice the traces, and the pair has to be routed together with matched lengths and constant spacing; if the two halves arrive at different times, some of the differential signal turns into common-mode noise, and that wrecks the benefit.
It also needs a differential receiver and usually a 100-ohm termination, and sometimes AC coupling with its own placement issues.
So I use differential where speed, noise or EMI demand it, and single-ended for slow, short, cheap nets."
